KEY MESSAGE 1...High pressure moves east to southeast of 
southeast New England this morning. Mid and high clouds continue
to increase across the region. In the west to northwest flow 
aloft associated with the long-wave trough over eastern Canada 
and an amplifying ridge over the central CONUS, a mid-level 
shortwave will move towards the region, as a weak warm front 
approaches from the south and west. The skies will become mostly
cloudy during the late morning through the afternoon and will 
thicken and lower. The weak forcing and modest low-level 
moisture convergence will allow for some isolated to scattered 
light showers to develop and we maintained the 20-40% PoPs from 
the Capital Region north and west, and kept 30-50% PoPs south 
and east. Some of the CAMs such as the 3-km NAM have a bit more 
coverage south and east of Albany today with some thunderstorms 
developing. The latest HREF guidance shows mean SBCAPEs mainly 
less than 500 J/kg south of the Capital District. The 0-6 km 
shear is 35-40 KT but the lack of instability should limit 
updraft height and strength, and mid level lapse rates remain 
weak. The thunderstorms are not expected to severe. We confined 
the slight chance of thunderstorms from about Hudson in Columbia
County south and east towards I-84. Max temps today were 
lowered about 2-4 degrees below the NBM values due to the mostly
cloudy conditions with highs in the upper 70s to about 80F in 
the major valleys, and mid 60s to mid 70s over the terrain. 

A cold front sinks southward across the region tonight into
Monday morning, as high pressure will build in. The scattered
showers and isolated t-storms end early. Some patchy fog 
especially in the major valleys and low stratus will develop and
were slightly expanded in the forecast. Lows will be in the 50s
to lower 60s. Most of the day Monday should remain dry with a 
1022 hPa or so sfc high building in from southern Quebec. By 
the afternoon, the stalled cold front over NY-PA may starts to 
lift back as a warm front and interact with a mid-leve short-
wave. Some showers may develop west of the Hudson River Valley 
in the mid to late pm. Temps will be seasonable in the 70s to 
around 80F with a few cooler readings over the mountains.

KEY MESSAGE 2...High pressure moves east of the region, as the
upstream ridging continues to increase over the Upper Midwest,
Great Lakes Region and Ontario with the closed anticyclone 
centered over the TN Valley and Southeast Mon night into 
Tue morning. A warm front slowly lifts north of the region Mon 
night for periods of showers/rain to develop due to the 
increasing isentropic lift. Some weak elevated instability is
present, so we placed a slight chance of t-storms from the 
Capital Region northward. An MCS/decaying MCS may move across 
the region. The rainfall may become briefly moderate to heavy, 
especially along and north of I-90, as PWATs rise above normal 
in the 1 to 2 STDEV range based on the NAEFS. WPC has the entire
region in Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 4) in ERO prior to 12Z/Tue.
Dry antecedent conditions should limit any widespread hydro 
threat, though some ponding of water on roadways and/or poor 
drainage flooding may occur in a few spots. Lows will be milder
in the upper 50s to mid 60s.

Tue through the mid-week continues to be a challenging and 
uncertain stretch of the forecast, as a few short-wave 
disturbances track around the rim of upstream ridge and impact 
the forecast area with showers and some strong to potentially 
severe thunderstorms. As the previous discussion mentioned, the 
timing of these disturbances with the diurnal heating and the 
placement of the front will be some of the keys for the robust 
threat of severe storms. The warm front and a weakening/decaying
MCS continues to move through Tuesday morning. Another 
impulse/short-wave may bring additional showers and isolated to
scattered thunderstorms on Tue based on the medium range 
guidance/AI/ensembles. Humidity levels will be on the increase 
with dewpoints in the 60s to close to 70F near POU, as max temps
will be near or above normal in the 70s to lower 80s. SPC did
include locations south and west of the Capital Region in a
Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5) in the Day 3 Outlook for potential
severe thunderstorms.  

Tue night into Wed, the guidance varies when a strong short-
wave could bring an MCS with strong/potentially severe t-storms 
to parts of the region with heavy rainfall. The latest GFS would
lean towards Tue night/Wed morning with some heavy rain of a 
few inches for locations along and north of I-90, while the EC 
and EC AI and some of the ensembles more in the Wed-Wed night 
time frame. WPC conditions ERO's D3 and D4 (Tue-Wed night) in 
the Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 4) for isolated flash 
flooding/heavy rainfall possible due to training/back building 
storms. A strong mid-level jet with 0-6 km shear close to 50 KT 
and some moderate/high instability could promote a more robust 
severe threat
